name: PCB Trace Current
seoDesc: PCB Trace Current: work out trace width from the trace thickness and the ambient temperature. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: The PCB Trace Current calculator turns the trace thickness, the ambient temperature and more into trace width. That makes it useful for whatever you happen to be working on. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the PCB Trace Current calculator work?
sections.html:
The PCB Trace Current calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports trace width in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the trace thickness, the ambient temperature, the length and the cross section.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as internal and external. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in square millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the PCB Trace Current calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Trace width=(500 ÷ 689) × cross section ÷ trace thickness
Max. desired temperature rise=-ambient temperature + trace temperature
Maximum current=(cross section ^ 29 ÷ 40) × (max. desired temperature rise ^ 11 ÷ 25) × the trace is...
Resistance=(17 ÷ 100000000000) × length × (39 × trace temperature + 9025) ÷ ((16129 ÷ 2500000000) × (cross section))
Resistance=voltage drop ÷ maximum current
Resistance=power dissipation ÷ (maximum current ^ 2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Temperature change, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Area, opening in square millimeters
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The PCB Trace Current calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the trace thickness, the ambient temperature and the length — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the PCB Trace Current calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns trace width, derived from the trace thickness, the ambient temperature and the length. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the PCB Trace Current calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the trace thickness, the ambient temperature, the length and the cross section, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter trace width in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Trace width opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the PCB Trace Current calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
